explanations: terra: The humble are certain both that they will meet their Lord and that they are returning to Him, combining the two ends named in 84:6 and the section.
terra: Abraham asks for a secure بلد and provision, while God says the unbeliever receives brief enjoyment before being driven to the Fire, joining settlement and supplies to divergent destinations.

luna: The section's b ل و note says testing can wear down what a person claims as his own; this ayah specifies fear, hunger, and loss of property, lives, and produce as tests. | terra: God promises testing through fear, hunger, and loss of wealth and lives; trial literally diminishes what the traveler thought was his.

luna: The preceding 2:155 lists losses in the test; this ayah gives the afflicted people's own response, إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ, joining trial to return. | terra: The tested people of 2:155 answer loss by saying they belong to God and are returning to Him, exactly joining attrition to return.
terra: True righteousness includes giving wealth despite love of it to kin, orphans, and the needy, reversing the section's conjunction of money-love and neglected dependents.

luna: The section moves from being tested toward a tranquil soul and entry into the Garden; this ayah describes earlier believers enduring hardship and upheaval before asking when God's help will come, making trial part of the passage toward that end.

luna: The section's root note defines tranquility as calm after disturbance; Abraham asks to see how God gives life so his heart may be reassured (لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي), a specific arrival at settled certainty. | terra: Abraham asks to see how the dead are revived so that his heart may become tranquil, joining settled heart, death, and return to life.

luna: The section explicitly warns that the proper name ʿĀd does not itself mean return, while its root note defines the true return; here عاد is an actual return to usury after warning, a relapse into wealth-seeking rather than the final return to God.

luna: The section focuses on love of wealth; this ayah lists gold, silver, and other desired possessions as attractions of worldly life, then sets the better return with God beyond them. | terra: Love of desires, including accumulated wealth and livestock, is worldly enjoyment, whereas the beautiful destination is with God.
terra: Righteousness is not reached until people spend from what they love, turning release of attachment into forward movement.
terra: Divine aid is made good news so that hearts may become tranquil through it, presenting calm as what follows fear and uncertainty.
terra: Believers are commanded to race toward forgiveness and a Garden, giving the final abode the force of a destination actively approached.
terra: People are commanded to travel through the earth and see the end of deniers, reading ruined predecessors as stations of warning.

luna: The section joins love of possessions to heaviness and binding; this ayah says what people withhold will be encircled around their necks on the Day of Resurrection, making attachment itself a restraint.

luna: The section's b ل و note pictures a journey wearing down what seems one's own; this ayah says believers will be tested in their property and selves (لَتُبْلَوُنَّ فِي أَمْوَالِكُمْ وَأَنفُسِكُمْ), making the test reach possessions directly. | terra: Believers are told that they will certainly be tested in their wealth and selves, the exact possessions and person that the section says trial abrades.

luna: The section's dictionary note on 89:9 evokes a man who crosses lands repeatedly; this ayah warns against being deceived by disbelievers' movement through the lands, since their apparent worldly mobility ends in loss.
luna: The preceding 3:196 warns against the disbelievers' movement through lands; this ayah supplies that movement's real endpoint, only brief enjoyment and then a wretched abode.

luna: The section likens attachment to a mount that will not rise; this ayah explicitly distinguishes those who stay seated (الْقَاعِدُونَ) from those who strive with their lives and property. | terra: Believers who sit without disability are not equal to those who strive with wealth and lives, making grounded nonmovement morally legible without condemning the unable.
terra: One who leaves home migrating to God and His messenger, then dies on the road, has already secured the reward; bodily travel can end before arrival while its direction remains decisive.

luna: The section's root note defines tranquility as settling after disturbance; after the prescribed prayer in fear, this ayah says when people become secure (اطْمَأْنَنتُمْ), they return to regular prayer.
terra: The disciples seek the table so their hearts may become tranquil and certainty may follow their unsettled question.
terra: On the truthful's Day, eternal gardens accompany God's pleasure with them and their pleasure with Him, linking mutual satisfaction to final abode.
terra: The command to journey through the earth and inspect the deniers' end makes travel itself a lesson in destination.

luna: The section's call is to return to the Lord; when the deniers see the Fire, they instead wish to be sent back to worldly life so they can believe, reversing the direction of return. | terra: When stationed before the Fire, the deniers wish to be sent back so they could respond differently, a failed request to reverse the finished route.

luna: The preceding 6:27 gives the deniers' wish to return; this ayah says that if they were sent back, they would repeat what they had been forbidden, closing that imagined route back. | terra: God says that if they were sent back they would return to what was forbidden, exposing moral repetition inside the desired physical return.
terra: Those who denied meeting God arrive suddenly at the Hour carrying their burdens on their backs, turning the journey's figurative load into a final visible weight.
terra: When warning is forgotten, every door of abundance is opened until people rejoice, then they are seized suddenly; provision functions as concealed testing.
terra: “As He began you, you will return” precisely matches the section's dictionary definition of return as going back to one's beginning.
terra: Heaven's gates do not open and entry to the Garden is impossible until a camel enters a needle's eye; mount, gate, and denied entry meet in one reversal.
terra: People once despised are commanded to enter the Garden without fear or grief, giving the lowly traveler the opposite of worldly humiliation.

luna: The section's return call leads the soul to God; those who forgot the final meeting instead ask whether they can be returned to act differently, a specific reversal of that completed passage. | terra: When judgment's interpretation arrives, deniers ask either for intercessors or to be returned so they can act differently, another too-late attempt to reverse the route.

luna: The section names Thamud cutting rock and refers to lands where people settle; this speech recalls their settlement after Aad and their carving houses from mountains (تَنْحِتُونَ الْجِبَالَ بُيُوتًا), a direct rock-and-dwelling parallel. | terra: Thamud are made successors after Aad and settled in the earth, building palaces and carving mountain homes; the section's named nations, lands, and grounded settlement meet in one verse.
terra: God afflicts towns that rejected prophets with hardship so they might humble themselves, making constriction an invitation rather than proof of humiliation.
terra: God replaces adversity with prosperity before seizing the heedless, so both conditions reveal rather than certify divine approval.
terra: God tests a dispersed people with good and bad “so that they might return,” uniting both kinds of trial with return.
luna: The section cites 7:176's person who clings to earth and follows desire; this preceding ayah explains his turn by saying he had been given signs but cast them off and followed Satan.

luna: The section itself cites أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ وَاتَّبَعَ هَوَاهُ: remaining attached to earth and following desire makes the earth-bound person the direct counter-image of the traveler. | terra: The bearer of signs clings to the earth and follows desire, a direct Qur'anic realization of the section's earthbound animal and person.
terra: The promise of angelic aid is given so hearts may become tranquil, again locating stillness after alarm in reliance on God.

luna: The section links the root ب ل و to what a person thinks is theirs; this ayah calls property and children a test (أَمْوَالُكُمْ وَأَوْلَادُكُمْ فِتْنَةٌ) and points beyond them to God's reward. | terra: Wealth and children are identified as a trial, turning what people cling to into the very instrument of testing.

luna: The section compares clinging to wealth with a mount that will not move; this ayah names family, property, and trade as more beloved than God, His Messenger, and striving in His path, making attachment the reason for staying back. | terra: Family, acquired wealth, feared commercial loss, and pleasing homes can be dearer than God and striving in His path; attachment directly prevents setting out.

luna: The section describes intense love of money and fixation on earthly possessions; this ayah names people who hoard gold and silver instead of spending in God's path, setting up the wealth that becomes punishment in 9:35.
luna: The preceding 9:34 names hoarded gold and silver; this ayah says that same wealth is heated and used to brand its owners, turning what they clung to into a bodily burden at judgment.

luna: The section itself names this reverse arrangement: ثَاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ is being heavy toward earth, followed by the question whether they prefer worldly life to the Hereafter, opposite the journey to God. | terra: The call to set out asks why believers grow heavy toward the earth and prefer the nearer life; it names the section's grounded refusal of the journey.

luna: The preceding 9:38 asks why believers cling to earth instead of the Hereafter; this ayah gives the warning's consequence: failure to go forth brings punishment and replacement by another people.

luna: The section's 9:38 image makes people heavy and fixed toward earth; this command reverses it with انْفِرُوا خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا, calling them to go forth in either condition and strive with wealth and selves. | terra: The command to set out light or heavy directly answers the earthward heaviness of 9:38 and makes weight no excuse for remaining fixed.
terra: A near gain and moderate journey would have drawn the reluctant, but distance burdens them, revealing how worldly calculation arrests setting out.
terra: Had the reluctant truly intended to set out, they would have prepared equipment; instead they are told to remain with those who sit.

luna: The section contrasts a journeying person with one fixed by attachment; these stay-behinds rejoice in remaining after the Messenger and dislike striving with their property and lives. | terra: Those left behind rejoice in sitting after the Messenger and dislike striving with wealth and selves, a social scene of attachment to place.
terra: When God returns the Prophet to some who stayed behind, they are barred from future departure because they chose sitting the first time.
terra: When commanded to believe and strive, the affluent ask permission to remain with those who sit, specifying privilege as a source of grounded refusal.
terra: They are content to remain with those left behind, so consent itself becomes the fastening that keeps them from the road.
terra: Those able to go nevertheless ask exemption and accept being among those left behind, repeating the grounded refusal knowingly.

luna: The section ends with entry among God's servants; this ayah describes the early believers as a group with whom God is pleased and for whom He has prepared gardens. | terra: God's pleasure with the first believers and their pleasure with Him are joined to gardens beneath which rivers flow and permanent residence.
luna: The section hears travel wearing down a mount; this ayah names thirst, fatigue, hunger, and every step taken in God's path as real costs that are counted as good deeds.
terra: Believers are explicitly told not all to set out; some remain to learn and warn their people, setting a boundary between necessary staying and earthbound refusal.
terra: Universal return to God is grounded in His beginning creation and repeating it, so destination and re-creation explain one another.

luna: The section's tranquil soul returns to its Lord; these people are satisfied with worldly life and settled into it (اطْمَأَنُّوا بِهَا), making worldly repose the opposite of the final repose. | terra: Those content with the nearer life become tranquil in it and neglect the signs; اطمئنان here is an earthbound settling opposite the Godward tranquil soul.
terra: The challenge asks who begins creation and repeats it, then answers that God does; the root ع و د supplies return as renewed origin rather than mere reversal of direction.
terra: God gives life and death and to Him people are returned, defining return across the full span of the journey.
terra: When mercy is withdrawn after being tasted, the human being becomes despairing and ungrateful, one half of the unstable reading of trial.
terra: When favor follows adversity, the person exults that troubles have left and becomes boastful, completing the fortune-governed response begun in 11:9.
terra: Those who desire worldly life and adornment may receive the full return of their deeds within it, but that payment does not make it the final abode.
terra: The world-seekers of 11:15 have only Fire in the Hereafter, exposing the destination hidden by complete worldly payment.
terra: Salih tells Thamud that God produced them from earth and settled them in it, then calls them to seek forgiveness and turn to Him.

luna: The section's root note on 89:4 is night travel; here Lot's household is ordered to leave at night (فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ), a second, urgent night departure. | terra: Lot is told to take his family through part of the night without anyone turning back, making direction and forbidden reversal part of the nocturnal journey.
terra: Joseph tells his traveling family to enter Egypt safely, a worldly reunion and secure entry that can illuminate the form, though not the final object, of the section's welcome.

luna: The section's traveler ranges from country to country; this ayah asks people to travel the earth and observe the end of earlier peoples, making travel an encounter with what remains after them. | terra: Travel through the earth is urged so that the end of earlier peoples can be seen, while the Hereafter is named as better for the God-fearing.
luna: The section ends with entry among God's servants; this ayah describes the Garden entered by the righteous and their righteous families, with angels coming to them from every gate.
luna: The preceding 13:23 shows the Garden and its entrants; this ayah gives the angels' welcome of peace for their patience and calls it an excellent final home.
terra: God guides to Himself whoever turns back to Him; this Godward turning immediately precedes the heart's tranquility in 13:28.

luna: The section explains the tranquil soul through stillness after disturbance and cites this source: remembrance of God is what makes hearts tranquil (تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ). | terra: Hearts find اطمئنان through God's remembrance, explicitly giving the source of the section's post-disturbance tranquility.

luna: The preceding 13:28 explains tranquil hearts; this ayah adds the believers' blessed state and good return (حُسْنُ مَآبٍ), joining inward rest to a destination. | terra: Those whose hearts become tranquil in 13:28 receive blessedness and a beautiful homecoming, so inner rest points toward final settlement.
terra: Those who prefer the nearer life over the Hereafter also obstruct God's way, joining worldly preference to blockage of the road.

terra: Abraham settles descendants in an uncultivated valley, asks that hearts incline toward them, and asks for provision, joining settlement, attachment, and sustenance without confusing any with the final home.
luna: The section's journey reaches its final return; this ayah gives wrongdoers' request for a short delay so they can answer the messengers, another too-late attempt to resume earthly life.
terra: On the final day criminals are seen bound together in fetters, giving the binding side of the section's journey-image its punitive destination.

luna: The section's last stage is entry; this ayah gives the Garden's direct welcome, ادْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ آمِنِينَ, marking safe arrival. | terra: The righteous are told to enter gardens in peace and security, a direct parallel to tranquil entry after the journey.
terra: The Garden's people suffer no fatigue and are never expelled, so arrival ends both weariness and further forced travel.

luna: The section's night-walking note meets Lot's departure: the command فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ sets a family on the road before dawn. | terra: Lot is told to set out by night, follow behind his family, forbid backward looking, and proceed where commanded.
luna: This passage opens with the people of the rocky dwellings (أَصْحَابَ الْحِجْرِ), the community whose mountain-cut houses continue the section's Thamud rock scene in 15:82.
luna: The section names Thamud as people who cut rock; this ayah says the people of the Hijr carved houses from mountains (يَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا).
luna: After 15:82 shows the carved mountain houses, this ayah says the people were seized by the cry in the morning, carrying the settled rock-city scene into its end.

luna: The preceding passage gives the carved dwellings and their destruction; this ayah says what they had earned did not avail them, linking the old settlement to the section's warning about possessions.

luna: The section's travel-worn mount becomes a concrete Quranic transport scene: livestock carry burdens to a distant بلد that people could reach only with hardship (بِشِقِّ الْأَنفُسِ). | terra: Livestock carry burdens to a بلد reachable only with severe hardship, directly joining the section's land-word to a journey-worn carrier.

luna: The preceding 16:7 gives beasts carrying burdens over a hard journey; this ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding, expanding the section's mount image. | terra: Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding and adornment, extending the burden-bearing journey of 16:7 into its family of mounts.

luna: The section's last stage is entry into the Garden; this ayah shows the angels welcoming the good at death with peace and the command to enter Paradise. | terra: Angels take the good in death, greet them with peace, and command them to enter the Garden, staging the section's final address at death.

luna: The section hears a traveler crossing countries; after describing messengers sent to every community, this ayah tells people to travel through the land and see the end of those who denied them. | terra: After recalling messengers sent to every community, the hearers are told to travel through the earth and see the deniers' end.
terra: After creation and death, some people are returned to decrepit age, making bodily life itself a wearing process rather than a secure possession.

luna: The section sets night travel and settling in place against one another; this ayah describes animal-skin dwellings made light for the day of travel and the day of stopping (ظَعْنِكُمْ … إِقَامَتِكُمْ), a portable answer to becoming fixed.
terra: A heart remains مطمئن in faith even under coercion, showing tranquility that survives external disturbance rather than depending on ease.
terra: Choosing the nearer life over the Hereafter explains rejection, making misplaced love a decision about destination.

terra: A secure, tranquil town receives ample provision from every direction, then ingratitude makes it taste the “garment” of hunger and fear; tranquility, provision, trial, settlement, and worn clothing converge.

luna: The section names 89:4 يَسْرِ as night walking; 17:1 uses أَسْرَىٰ … لَيْلًا for God carrying His servant by night, giving the image a divinely directed night journey. | terra: God takes His servant by night from one sanctuary to another, the explicit Qur'anic night journey evoked by يَسْرِ.
terra: Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God wills and then reaches Hell, showing worldly preference determining a ruinous endpoint.
terra: Whoever wants the Hereafter, strives toward it properly, and believes has that striving accepted, supplying the positive route opposite 17:18.

luna: The section names Thamud and develops a camel image beside testing; this ayah recalls that Thamud received the she-camel as a clear sign but wronged it, joining the named people, camel, and test.
terra: God carries Adam's children on land and sea and provides good things, framing human mobility and supplies as conferred honor rather than ownership.
terra: The earth's adornment is made a test of deeds, so attractive earthly possession is explicitly temporary testing material.
luna: The section says a person can cling to wealth as though it were his own; the garden-owner boasts that he has more wealth (أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا), giving that attachment a concrete speaker.

luna: The preceding 18:34 gives the wealthy owner's boast; this ayah shows him entering his garden while wronging himself and denying that it will ever perish, exposing the false permanence of what he owns. | terra: The garden owner enters his possession and asserts that it will never perish, treating a temporary station as permanent settlement.

luna: The section names return to the Lord as the true destination; the wealthy owner imagines, وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي, that even a return would bring him something better, reversing humble return into entitlement. | terra: He doubts the Hour yet assumes that, if returned to his Lord, he will find an even better destination, corrupting return into entitlement.

luna: The preceding garden narrative shows a man trusting his wealth; this ayah says the crop is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, a concrete case of possessions passing away. | terra: The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent, visibly wearing away what he thought securely his.

luna: The section's dictionary note says a garment wears out and a mount is consumed by travel; this ayah pictures worldly life as vegetation that becomes dry debris scattered by wind, a specific image of what seemed substantial passing away. | terra: Worldly life is vegetation that flourishes after rain and then becomes wind-scattered debris, a visible account of what use and time wear away.

luna: The section's loved wealth is something people cling to; this ayah calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life, then says lasting good deeds are better with the Lord. | terra: Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring deeds are better with the Lord, distinguishing what the traveler carries from what remains at arrival.
luna: The section connects the ground's final crushing with return; this ayah describes the mountains moved, the earth laid bare, and all people gathered, joining altered landscape to final assembly.
terra: Moses refuses to stop until he reaches the meeting of the seas even if he travels for ages, opposing the section's creature that settles and will not rise.

luna: The section's dictionary image of a travel-worn mount has a human counterpart: after their journey Moses and his companion say, لَقَدْ لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا, describing the journey's fatigue. | terra: After passing the appointed place, Moses explicitly says that the journey has caused weariness, the human counterpart to the worn mount.
terra: Moses and his servant return along their own tracks, staging return as literal travel back toward a missed starting point.
terra: Those abiding in Paradise desire no transfer from it, explicitly marking the destination as the end of relocation.
terra: The God-fearing are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation, a dignified caravan that sharpens the companies driven to the Garden.
terra: Criminals are driven thirsty to Hell, providing the opposed caravan and destination to the delegation in 19:85.
terra: God creates humans from earth, returns them into it, and brings them out again; return here is literally to the material point of beginning.

luna: The section names the root س ر ي for night travel; Moses is told أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي, so the root becomes a collective escape route from Pharaoh. | terra: Moses is commanded to take God's servants by night and strike a dry road through the sea, joining night departure, travelers, and an opened path.
luna: The section's earth is crushed at the end; this ayah answers a question about the mountains by saying the Lord will blow them away, extending the scene from earth to its fixed high landmarks.
luna: The preceding 20:105 says the mountains will be blown away; this ayah says the land is left as a level plain, completing the landscape's removal of height and support.
luna: After 20:105 and 20:106 describe mountains removed and a level plain, this ayah says no crookedness or elevation will remain, making the emptied terrain explicit.
terra: The bloom of worldly life given to groups is itself a test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting.

luna: The section connects being tested with the road back to God; this ayah says people are tested with good and evil (نَبْلُوكُم بِالشَّرِّ وَالْخَيْرِ) and ends, وَإِلَيْنَا تُرْجَعُونَ. | terra: Every soul tastes death, is tested through evil and good, and is returned to God; this states the section's whole sequence of wearing trial and return.
terra: The greatest terror does not grieve the faithful; angels receive them with the announcement that this is their promised day.
terra: God promises to repeat creation just as He began the first creation, giving the journey's return a cosmic scale.

luna: The section's soul is tranquil at the journey's end; this ayah describes a person who is reassured only when good comes (اطْمَأَنَّ بِهِ) and turns back when tested, a conditional and unstable counterpart. | terra: A person at the edge is reassured by good but turns away under trial; this reverses the tranquil soul by exposing a calm dependent on fortune.

luna: The section hears a road-worn she-camel beside its account of testing; the pilgrimage call brings people on foot and on every lean camel (ضَامِرٍ), a specific arduous journey by mount. | terra: Pilgrims arrive on every lean camel from every distant pass; the lean body makes travel's wearing of the mount visible.
luna: The section names ancient settled lands and rock-cut places; this ayah describes ruined towns, an abandoned well, and a lofty palace, giving the traveler concrete traces of vanished settlement.

luna: The preceding 22:45 shows ruined towns and abandoned structures; this ayah asks whether people have traveled the land and gained understanding from what happened, linking the traveler to the ruins. | terra: Journeying through the earth is meant to produce understanding hearts and hearing ears amid the remains of destroyed settlements.
terra: Livestock give drink and many benefits, so the mount is also provision rather than merely property that belongs to its rider.
terra: People are carried on livestock and ships, making the mortal traveler a passenger on means supplied to him.
terra: The question challenges the belief that continued wealth and sons necessarily signify favor, directly exposing the error dramatized in 89:15.
terra: What people mistake for hastened good in 23:55 is explicitly denied, separating bestowed abundance from divine approval.

luna: The section's r ج ع note describes a return to the beginning-place; at death the denier instead begs, رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ, to be sent back into worldly life, the opposite direction. | terra: At death the unbeliever asks his Lord to send him back, seeking another journey only when the allotted one has ended.

luna: The preceding 23:99 is a plea to return; this ayah answers with كَلَّا, the same response word the section notes in Surah 89, and says the plea will not reopen the completed journey. | terra: The answer is كَلَّا: the request of 23:99 is only a spoken word, and a barrier prevents return until resurrection.
terra: The question denies that humans were created pointlessly or would fail to be returned, making return the purpose-bearing completion of creation.
terra: The Garden's people have the better settled place and the finer resting place, giving the journey a true rest rather than earthbound stagnation.
terra: The patient are rewarded with a lofty chamber and received there with greeting and peace, another final welcome after endurance.
terra: Their dwelling is permanent and praised as both settlement and residence, distinguishing arrival from a temporary stop.

luna: The section's night-walking root recurs in the command أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي; this is Moses leading the people away while pursuit is expected. | terra: God commands Moses to take His servants by night because they will be pursued, casting the night journey as a departure under pressure.

luna: The section's return is a completed journey to the Lord; here the deniers, seeing the punishment, wish they could return to become believers, a late reversal that cannot restore the road. | terra: The condemned wish for one more return so they could become believers, stating the impossible repeated journey in a single request.
luna: In the continuing story of Aad, this ayah asks whether they build a sign on every high place (آيَةً بِكُلِّ رِيعٍ), recalling the monumental landscape beside Iram's pillars in the section.

luna: The section's old cities seem fixed and enduring; Aad's people take fortresses (مَصَانِعَ) as if they might abide forever, a direct false-permanence parallel to the journey's eventual end. | terra: Aad construct great works as though they might remain forever, giving monumental form to the desire to settle permanently in the passing world.
luna: The section says earlier peoples transgressed in the lands; this ayah describes Aad's violence as tyrannical whenever they seized someone (بَطَشْتُم بَطَشْتُمْ جَبَّارِينَ).
luna: The section's Thamud scene centers on cutting rock; this ayah says they carved houses from mountains with skill and pride (تَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا فَارِهِينَ).
terra: Solomon names extraordinary provision as his Lord's test of gratitude or ingratitude, correcting the claim that bestowed abundance simply proves honor.

luna: The section's country-crossing traveler is told in another passage to travel through the earth and see the end of the guilty, directly turning movement across lands into a view of their fate. | terra: Travel through the earth and observation of criminals' end turn the country-crossing traveler into a witness of where rebellion leads.
terra: Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting, distinguishing supplies from destination.

luna: The section joins attachment to wealth with heaviness toward earth; Qarun's treasure is so vast that its keys weigh on a company of strong men (لَتَنُوءُ بِالْعُصْبَةِ), a specific image of riches as burden.
terra: The recipient of wealth is told to seek the Hereafter through what God gave while using his worldly share well, turning possession into provisions for the destination.

luna: The preceding 28:76 describes Qarun's immense treasure; this ayah says the earth swallowed him and his dwelling (فَخَسَفْنَا بِهِ وَبِدَارِهِ الْأَرْضَ), making wealth's weight a literal collapse into earth. | terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, making worldly attachment culminate in literal earthward engulfment.
terra: After Qarun's fall, his former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that abundance did not prove favor.

luna: The section's dictionary note calls مَعَاد a place of return; this ayah promises the Prophet, لَرَادُّكَ إِلَىٰ مَعَادٍ, a return to the appointed destination. | terra: The One who imposed the Qur'an promises the Prophet that He will return him to a مَعَاد, explicitly naming return as an appointed destination.
terra: People are asked to see how God begins creation and repeats it; 29:20 then turns that insight into a journey through the earth.

luna: The section's traveling person moves across the earth; this ayah explicitly joins travel through it with observing how creation began and how God will bring forth the later creation, linking the route to origin and return. | terra: The command to travel through the earth and observe how creation began links traversing lands to the final, next creation.

luna: The section names both Aad and Thamud and their settled lands; this ayah names the same peoples, points to their dwellings, and says Satan turned them from the path despite their insight. | terra: The dwellings of Aad and Thamud remain visible, yet Satan blocked them from the way despite their discernment; fixed habit becomes obstruction of the road.
terra: “My servants” are told that God's earth is spacious and to worship Him, making movement through the earth the prelude to the section's final summons among the servants.
terra: After the servants are told to move through God's broad earth in 29:56, every soul tastes death and is returned to Him.
terra: The believers who travel, die, and return in 29:56-57 are lodged permanently in lofty Garden chambers, completing the journey with settlement.
terra: Travelers in a ship call sincerely on God in danger, then associate partners after He delivers them to land, so safe ground becomes the place of renewed forgetfulness.
terra: Those who strive toward God are promised guidance along His ways, joining exertion, direction, and divine accompaniment.

luna: The section joins travel across lands to old settled powers; this ayah asks people to travel and look at the fate of earlier peoples who cultivated the land more extensively, yet were destroyed after rejecting messengers. | terra: Travelers are told to inspect the fate of stronger predecessors who cultivated and built the earth; settled power did not prevent the journey's end.

luna: The section says ر ج ع is going back to where one began; this ayah joins God beginning creation, repeating it, and people's return to Him (ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ). | terra: God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him, an exact sequence from origin through return to destination.
terra: The command to travel and view earlier peoples' end connects traversal of countries with the repeated consequences of shirk.
terra: God creates from weakness, grants strength, then returns strength to weakness and gray age, describing the traveler's embodied arc as renewed attrition.

luna: The section's return-call brings the soul to the Lord; these condemned people instead ask, رَبَّنَا أَخِّرْنَا, for more earthly time to act, reversing the final return into a request to delay it. | terra: At judgment the guilty ask to be returned so they can act rightly, another final-arrival scene in which a new outward journey is too late.
luna: The preceding 32:12 asks for delay; this ayah answers that the decision is settled and that Hell will be filled, giving the refusal that completes the failed request to return.
terra: God places visible settlements along a measured route and commands safe travel through them by nights and days, a direct map of journey stages through lands.
terra: The travelers ask that their journeys be lengthened and are scattered into tales, turning the measured road of 34:18 into loss and dispersal.
terra: The affluent claim that superior wealth and children mean they will not be punished, the same false inference from provision to honor.
terra: The Prophet is told to answer that God expands and restricts provision as He wills, directly matching the two conditions misread in 89:15-16.
terra: Wealth and children do not bring people near to God; faith and action, rather than possessions, determine nearness and reward.
terra: No burdened soul bears another's load, even a heavily laden person cannot transfer it, and the verse ends by naming God as the destination.
terra: The people of the lasting Garden are clothed in silk after arrival; this may faintly reverse the source section's dictionary image of a garment worn out by use.
terra: At the lasting abode the travelers say that no fatigue or weariness touches them, so the worn journey ends rather than beginning another.

luna: The section contrasts the tranquil soul's return with the denier's rejected request; here the condemned ask to be brought out so they can act righteously, and are told they had ample life and warning. | terra: The inhabitants of the Fire cry to be taken out so they can act rightly, but their completed lifespan and warning make the requested new journey unavailable.

luna: The section's roaming traveler passes through lands marked by earlier powers; this ayah likewise asks people to travel and consider the end of those before them, showing that greater strength did not let them escape God. | terra: Travel is commanded so people can see how stronger predecessors ended, denying that established power can halt the route to judgment.
terra: Shackles reaching to the chins hold rejecters with heads forced up, giving the section's binding image a scene of bodily immobilization.
terra: The believer asks why he should not worship his Creator when everyone will be returned to Him, relating origin, allegiance, and end.
terra: The slain believer is directly told to enter the Garden, a singular death-side welcome closely parallel to the soul's command in surah 89.
terra: God could efface their eyes so they race blindly for the path and cannot see it; 36:67 then removes even their power to advance or return.
terra: Those fixed in their places can neither go forward nor return, directly staging the motionless mount and the blocked return together.
terra: Whoever is granted long life is reversed in creation, a bodily counterpart to the mount and garment worn through continued use.

luna: The section says Pharaoh's stake (أَوْتَاد) pins a foot to earth; this ayah repeats the specific title فِرْعَوْنُ ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ in the account of earlier deniers. | terra: Pharaoh is again called “owner of the stakes,” confirming the stake as the emblem attached to the tyrant named in the section.
terra: The God-fearing are promised a beautiful homecoming, naming the quality of the destination before its doors appear in 38:50.
terra: Everlasting gardens stand with their gates opened to the arriving God-fearing, paralleling the opened-gate entry in 39:73.
terra: Believing servants are told to fear their Lord and reminded that God's earth is spacious, making migration through the earth part of faithful perseverance.
terra: When hardship touches a person he calls on God, but after a favor he claims it came through his own knowledge; God calls the favor itself a test.
terra: God addresses prodigal people as “My servants” and forbids despair, opening a return while the journey can still change.
terra: The servants are commanded to turn back to their Lord and submit before punishment arrives, the timely counterpart to the denied request in 23:99.
luna: The section describes the soul returning to its Lord; this ayah gives the condemned person's wish for another return so he might become one of the good-doers.
luna: The preceding 39:58 gives the wish for another return; this ayah answers that God's signs had already come and were denied, giving the reason the request cannot reopen the journey.

luna: The section's final caravan enters the Garden in 39:73; this verse gives the opposing procession, disbelievers driven in groups toward Hell. | terra: Disbelievers too are driven in groups and told to enter, but their caravan reaches Hell; its mirrored staging sharpens the destination in 39:73.
luna: The preceding 39:71 shows the condemned arriving in groups; this ayah has Hell's gates opened and commands them to enter, completing the opposite destination to 39:73.

luna: The section calls entry the last stage of the journey; this ayah shows the God-fearing being led in groups to the Garden (إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ زُمَرًا) and welcomed at its open gates. | terra: The God-fearing are conducted in companies to the Garden and told at its opened gates to enter forever, the section's final entry as a completed caravan.
terra: After entering in 39:73, the travelers praise God and take their place wherever they wish in the Garden's land, explicitly turning arrival into settlement.
terra: After confessing two deaths and two lives, the condemned ask whether there is any path out, explicitly seeking a road away from the final destination.

luna: The section evokes a traveler crossing lands and recalls ancient powers; this ayah asks people to travel the earth and see the end of earlier peoples, whose strength and traces did not protect them from judgment. | terra: Those who journey through the earth can see the end of predecessors stronger in power and traces, a parallel to surah 89's powerful ruined peoples.
terra: The believer contrasts the world's brief enjoyment with the Hereafter as the home of settled residence, distinguishing the roadside from the abode.
terra: God appoints livestock so that people ride some and eat from others, locating the mount among gifts rather than possessions secured by the self.
terra: Needs are attained through livestock, and people are carried on them and on ships, broadening the section's one exhausted mount into all human transport.

luna: This repeated travel-and-observe formulation says earlier peoples had greater numbers, strength, and traces in the land, but their earnings did not avail them, connecting monumental settlement to what cannot be retained. | terra: Travelers are again told to inspect the fate of the more numerous and stronger predecessors whose acquisitions did not benefit them.
luna: The section names Aad and says earlier peoples transgressed in the lands; this ayah says Aad became arrogant on earth without right (اسْتَكْبَرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ).
luna: The preceding 41:15 describes Aad's arrogance on earth; this ayah gives the destructive wind sent against them, a specific outcome for the land-transgressors named in the section.
luna: The section also names Thamud; this ayah turns to them, says they preferred blindness to guidance, and describes the humiliating thunderbolt that seized them.

luna: The section presents a soul arriving tranquil and welcomed; this ayah describes the angels reassuring those who remained steadfast and giving them glad tidings of the Garden. | terra: Angels descend upon the steadfast, remove fear and grief, and announce the promised Garden, a close communal parallel to the tranquil soul's final welcome.
terra: A person tirelessly asks for good but becomes despairing when adversity touches him, exposing a soul whose state is governed by provision.
terra: After mercy follows adversity, the person calls it his own, doubts the Hour, and assumes a fine return, combining possession, denial of the journey's end, and false confidence.
terra: Seeking the Hereafter's harvest increases it, while seeking the world's harvest yields a portion with no share in the Hereafter; desire selects what the journey produces.
terra: Whatever people receive is worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for those who trust Him.
terra: When wrongdoers see punishment they ask whether there is any way of return, a final search for a road back after arrival.
luna: The section's road across lands meets the description of earth as a resting-place with paths placed through it (سُبُلًا لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ): earth is made traversable and gives direction.

luna: The section joins a mount to the return journey; the following ayat develop that scene, and this ayah supplies the animals and ships made into means of transport. | terra: God creates the pairs and appoints ships and cattle as mounts, placing the section's worn mount inside a divinely furnished journey.

luna: After 43:12 names mounts, this ayah has riders settle on their backs and remember their Lord (عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهَا); it joins travel with acknowledgment at the moment of riding. | terra: The rider settles on the mount's back and remembers the One who subjected it, correcting the possessive attachment that the section says trial wears away.

luna: The section's road ends in return to the Lord; after describing the mount, this ayah says إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ, explicitly making the ride a reminder of return. | terra: The mount prayer ends, “to our Lord we shall return,” joining vehicle, journey, and final return in one scene.
terra: “My servants” are addressed with freedom from fear and grief, the communal welcome corresponding to the tranquil soul's address.
terra: The servants addressed in 43:68 are identified as those who believed and submitted, specifying who receives the welcome.
terra: The welcomed servants are commanded to enter the Garden rejoicing, closely matching “enter among My servants” and “enter My Garden.”

luna: The section's root note on 89:4 is enacted in أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي لَيْلًا: a night departure that carries the people toward safety while they are pursued. | terra: The command to take God's servants by night because they will be pursued repeats the section's opening movement as a communal exodus.
terra: God destroyed towns around the hearers and varied the signs “so that they might return,” joining ruined lands like those in surah 89 to the call back.

luna: The section names former powers and their lands; this ayah asks people to travel and observe how God destroyed earlier peoples, making the route through the land a lesson in their end. | terra: Travel through the earth reveals the destroyed end of earlier deniers and warns that present disbelief has the same destination.

luna: The section's beloved wealth pins a person in place; these stay-behinds say their property and families occupied them (شَغَلَتْنَا أَمْوَالُنَا وَأَهْلُونَا), making attachment the stated reason they did not travel. | terra: The desert Arabs claim that wealth and families kept them occupied, giving possessions as the stated reason for remaining behind a commanded journey.

luna: The section's final movement is entry into the Garden; this neighboring passage says the Garden is brought near to the God-fearing (أُزْلِفَتِ الْجَنَّةُ), depicting arrival before the invitation in 50:34. | terra: The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing rather than remaining distant, beginning the arrival scene completed by entry in 50:34.

luna: The section describes return and entry; this ayah identifies the promised Garden as the outcome for every returning, watchful person (أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ), joining return to the destination. | terra: The promised Garden belongs to every repeatedly returning, watchful person, identifying return as the disposition of the traveler welcomed in 50:33-34.

luna: The preceding 50:32 speaks of every returning person; this ayah describes one who comes with a heart returning to God (قَلْبٍ مُّنِيبٍ), the inward counterpart of the section's tranquil soul. | terra: The promised traveler comes with a heart that repeatedly turns back, preparing the inner posture for the entry commanded in 50:34.

luna: The section ends with a command to enter among God's servants; this ayah gives the Garden's arrival command, ادْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ, and names it the day of abiding. | terra: “Enter it in peace” names entry, safety, and the day of permanent abiding as the end of the returning heart's road.
terra: God gives life and death and to Him is the destination, linking the whole mortal interval to its terminus.
terra: “Flee to God” turns return into urgent directed motion and identifies God Himself as refuge and destination.
terra: The Prophet is told to turn from one who wants only the nearer life, identifying exclusive worldly desire as a refusal of further direction.
terra: No burden-bearer carries another's burden, establishing the personal load whose corresponding effort is named in 53:39.
terra: A human being has only what he strives for, closely paralleling the strenuous movement toward the Lord in 84:6.
terra: Each person's striving will be seen, so no stage of the journey's labor disappears at arrival.
terra: The seen striving is fully repaid before 53:42 names the Lord as the final limit.
terra: The final limit is to the Lord, an exceptionally concise statement of where the section's road ends.

luna: The section's b ل و note evokes a she-camel worn by travel, while this ayah sends Thamud a she-camel as a test (النَّاقَةِ فِتْنَةً لَّهُمْ); the shared animal and trial meet in a distinct Quranic scene. | terra: God sends the she-camel itself as a test, unexpectedly joining the section's camel image to its explicit theme of trial.
terra: The one brought near receives rest and fragrant provision, preparing the Garden welcome stated in 56:89.
terra: At death the near one is received with rest, fragrance, and a Garden of bliss, a compact arrival after mortal exertion.

luna: The section says testing can wear down what a person thinks is his; this ayah compares worldly life to growth that yellows and becomes debris, contrasting temporary possession with the lasting Hereafter. | terra: Worldly rivalry in wealth and children is compared to vegetation that delights, withers, yellows, and becomes debris; possession visibly ages like the section's garment and mount.
terra: The command to race toward forgiveness and the Garden casts faithful life as a contest whose finish is divine pardon and abode.
terra: God is pleased with the faithful and they are pleased with Him, and they are named God's party, extending mutual satisfaction beyond solitary feeling into belonging.
terra: Every soul is told to inspect what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, making deeds advance provisions to the destination before the traveler arrives.

luna: The section's return is the road's endpoint; this ayah gives a dying person the opposite wish, رَبِّ لَوْلَا أَخَّرْتَنِي, hoping for more time to give charity and become righteous. | terra: At the coming of death, a person asks for a short delay in order to give and become righteous, seeking extra travel-time only at the endpoint.

luna: The preceding 63:10 asks for delay; this ayah says God will not delay a soul when its term arrives, a boundary on the wish to resume the journey. | terra: God never delays a soul when its appointed time arrives, closing the extension requested in 63:10.

luna: The section's test image reaches what people possess; this repeated formulation calls property and children a trial (فِتْنَةٌ) and sets God's great reward beyond them. | terra: Wealth and children are only a trial, while the great reward is with God; possession becomes a stage rather than the destination.
terra: Pharaoh's wife asks her Lord to build her a house near Him in the Garden, defining final settlement by nearness to the Lord rather than earthly palace.
terra: Death and life are created to test which person acts best, placing the whole mortal journey inside a trial.

luna: The section contrasts walking with clinging to earth; this ayah makes earth traversable (فَامْشُوا فِي مَنَاكِبِهَا), provides sustenance, and ends with resurrection to God, linking road, provision, and destination. | terra: People are told to walk through the earth, eat God's provision, and know that resurrection is to Him; travel, provision, and destination form one itinerary.
terra: The owners of the garden are tested as earlier people were tested, and the owned garden becomes the means by which their claim to possession is worn down.
terra: The tested owners' garden becomes like a dark, harvested field overnight, making the attrition announced in 68:17 visible.
terra: The owners finally confess that they have been deprived, discovering through loss that possession and provision were never guaranteed.
luna: The section names Aad and Thamud among the settled powers; this ayah names both together (ثَمُودُ وَعَادٌ) in the account of the overwhelming blow against earlier deniers.
luna: The preceding 69:4 names Thamud and Aad; this ayah specifies Thamud's destruction by the overwhelming blast, completing one side of the section's paired peoples.
luna: The preceding passage names Aad; this ayah gives their destruction by a furious wind (بِرِيحٍ صَرْصَرٍ), a concrete fate for one of the section's old powers.
luna: The preceding 69:6 names the wind against Aad; this ayah describes it lasting seven nights and eight days and leaving people fallen, extending the scene of their disappearance.
luna: After the wind account against Aad, this ayah asks whether any remnant of them is seen, making the ruined power and empty land explicit.
luna: The section's 89:21 context crushes the earth at the end; this ayah gives a parallel scene in which the earth and mountains are lifted and crushed in one blow.
terra: The recipient of the right-hand record enters a “pleasing life,” echoing the root of the pleased soul at arrival.
terra: That pleasing life is located in a lofty Garden, supplying the abode for the satisfaction named in 69:21.
terra: The arrivals eat and drink because of what they sent ahead in past days, presenting final provision as the fruit of advance preparation.
terra: The condemned is seized and shackled at arrival, the immobilized opposite of the tranquil soul freely commanded to enter.
terra: He is inserted into a long chain, completing the binding sequence begun in 69:30.
terra: The human being is created anxiously unstable, introducing the opposed reactions to adversity and good in 70:20-21.
terra: When harm touches him he panics, paralleling the mistaken humiliation inferred from restricted provision.
terra: When good touches him he withholds it, joining favorable provision to the clinging refusal to release possessions.
luna: The section's earth can be a weight that holds a person down; this ayah instead says God spread it out (بِسَاطًا), and 71:20 gives the purpose: people travel its broad routes.
luna: The section pictures a person stuck to earth; this continuation says earth was spread so people may travel its broad ways (سُبُلًا فِجَاجًا), turning the same ground into a route.
terra: Some people travel through the earth seeking God's bounty, a direct Qur'anic instance of the country-crossing traveler whose road is tied to provision.

luna: The section describes the road's end as a place of settling; this ayah names the final resting-place as إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ. | terra: On that day the settled destination, ٱلْمُسْتَقَرّ, is to the Lord, so the journey ends in abiding before Him.
terra: The rebuke says that people love the immediate life; 75:21 completes the motion by saying they leave the Hereafter behind.
terra: Leaving the Hereafter accompanies love of the immediate in 75:20, showing how attachment determines which end of the journey is abandoned.
terra: God guides the human being to the way and leaves gratitude or ingratitude as the response, joining direction to the trial of received gifts.
terra: Chains, shackles, and a blaze await rejecters, turning the section's brief binding image into a final state of enforced immobility.
terra: The righteous feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite love of the food, showing love loosened rather than used as an anchor.
terra: Patience is rewarded with a Garden and silk, allowing the source section's worn mount and garment to end in enduring shelter and clothing.
terra: People love the immediate life and leave behind them a heavy day, combining attachment, neglect of the destination, and the section's imagery of weight.
luna: The section's peg image is a human stake driven into the ground; this ayah calls mountains pegs (أَوْتَادًا), shifting the same fastening image from Pharaoh's power to the created landscape.
terra: On the true Day, whoever wills is invited to take a homeward course toward the Lord, expressing destination as a route deliberately chosen.
terra: On the great emergence a person remembers what he strove for, bringing the whole road's effort into awareness before the two destinations are disclosed.
terra: The one whose destination is Fire is first identified by transgression, supplying the moral movement behind the worldly preference of 79:38.
terra: The transgressor prefers the nearer life, the same choice named in the section's earthbound call.
terra: Hell becomes the transgressor's shelter after his preference in 79:38, showing attachment ending in a contrary abode.
terra: The person who fears standing before the Lord restrains the self from desire, reversing the worldly preference described in 79:38.
terra: The Garden becomes the shelter of the desire-restraining traveler, completing the alternative destination to 79:39.
terra: At the final upheaval prized pregnant camels are abandoned, showing that even the most valued mount and possession cannot be carried beyond the journey.
luna: The section's earth is heavy and is crushed at the journey's end; this ayah gives the contrary end-time scene of the earth being stretched out (مُدَّتِ الْأَرْضُ).
luna: The preceding 84:3 spreads the earth; this ayah says it throws out what is within and empties itself, continuing the collapse of the settled ground.
luna: The preceding verses describe the earth laid bare; this ayah says it listens to its Lord's command, turning the land itself toward the final summons.

luna: The section says the road-worn mount and return call meet in one person; this ayah makes the human the traveler, كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا, laboring toward the Lord and meeting Him. | terra: Human life is strenuous movement toward the Lord and ends in meeting Him, making the section's journey an account of all human effort.
terra: The joyful worldling thought that he would never return, directly opposing the strenuous meeting with the Lord announced in 84:6.
terra: God begins and repeats creation; the ع و د wording keeps the section's final return tied to renewal even without a travel scene.
terra: People prefer the nearer life, directly naming the choice that makes the traveler cling to the present ground.
terra: The Hereafter is better and more lasting than what is preferred in 87:16, defining the true destination by permanence.
terra: Radiant faces are pleased with their striving, joining arduous effort to satisfaction at its result.
terra: Those pleased with their striving in 88:9 are in a lofty Garden, locating that satisfaction at the journey's end.
terra: The Qur'an directs attention to how the camel was created; the section's lexicographic camel-image thus points back to a creature made for contemplation.
terra: The return of all people is to God, followed by their reckoning, stating the compulsory homeward direction of the journey.
terra: Humanity is created in toil, supporting the section's presentation of mortal life as an arduous passage rather than settled ease.
luna: The section names Thamud and connects testing with a female camel; this ayah says Thamud denied the truth in their transgression (بِطَغْوَاهَا), setting the camel episode in its moral context.
luna: The preceding ayah names Thamud's transgression; this ayah says their most wretched man sprang forward, the act that leads into the warning about the she-camel in 91:13.

luna: The section's camel is a travel-worn mount, while this continuation names Allah's she-camel and its allotted drink (نَاقَةَ اللَّهِ وَسُقْيَاهَا), a distinct but specific camel scene among Thamud.

luna: The preceding 91:13 sets the she-camel boundary; this ayah says they denied and hamstrung her, after which their Lord destroyed them, connecting the Thamud scene to the section's doomed old powers.
terra: When one task is finished, the addressee is told to continue laboring, keeping exertion continuous until its orientation is named in 94:8.
terra: Desire is directed toward the Lord after renewed labor in 94:7, assigning the traveler's effort its proper end.

luna: The section names return to the Lord as the destination; this ayah states it as an unavoidable endpoint: إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَىٰ. | terra: The warning “to your Lord is the return” addresses the self-sufficient transgressor, matching the section's return-address to the soul after worldly attachment.

luna: The section's final soul is pleased and pleasing as it returns to God; this ayah joins God's pleasure with the believers' pleasure and promises them lasting gardens. | terra: Eternal gardens culminate in God being pleased with the faithful and their being pleased with Him, directly expanding رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً.
luna: The section links a person to earth's weight and final crushing; this ayah reverses stable ground into earth shaken by its quake (زُلْزِلَتِ الْأَرْضُ زِلْزَالَهَا).

luna: The preceding 99:1 shakes the earth; this ayah says it brings out its burdens (أَثْقَالَهَا), making the earth's weight and release a direct continuation. | terra: The earth casts out its burdens at the last convulsion, reversing the person who tried to grow heavy and remain attached to it.
luna: After the earth shakes and releases its burdens, this ayah gives humanity's startled question about what has happened to it, the human response to the upheaval.
luna: The preceding verses establish the earth's shaking and humanity's question; this ayah says the earth will report its news, making the ground disclose what it carried.
luna: The preceding 99:4 says the earth will speak; this ayah says its Lord inspired it, completing the scene of earth answering the final command.

luna: The section's love image is attachment to money; the oath-surah says a person is intense in love of wealth (لِحُبِّ الْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ), a direct formulation of that attachment. | terra: The human being's intense love of wealth directly repeats the attachment named in 89:20 before the surah turns to the graves.
terra: The person with heavy scales enters a pleasing life, a further use of satisfaction for the state reached after judgment.

luna: The section's money-lover remains attached to what he has; this ayah says rivalry in accumulation (التَّكَاثُرُ) distracts people, naming the force that keeps them occupied. | terra: Competitive accumulation distracts travelers from their end until the grave-visit of 102:2.

luna: The preceding 102:1 names distraction by accumulation; this ayah carries it to the graves (حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ), giving attachment a finite endpoint. | terra: The distracted accumulators finally visit the graves, making death the unavoidable stop that wealth-love had hidden.

luna: The section's intense love of money is made concrete in the person who gathers wealth and counts it (جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ). | terra: The condemned person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, enacting the clinging possessiveness of the section.
terra: He imagines that wealth has made him permanent, a direct false reversal of the journey toward death and return.
terra: The winter and summer journeys make repeated seasonal travel the condition of Quraysh's settled security and provision.
